title: Environmental view and color for a simulated telemarketing task✩
research_question: To determine the effects of task type (low/high demand), environmental color (red/blue), environmental view (scenic picture present/absent), and breaks (present/absent) on mood, satisfaction, motivation, and performance in a simulated telemarketing task.

participants.description: 128 undergraduate students (32 male, 96 female; ages 18-25, median 19) for Experiment 1. 128 undergraduate students (36 male, 92 female; ages 17-28, median 19) for Experiment 2. All from a mid-sized, private mid-western university in the United States.
participants.recruitment: Volunteered for course credit in psychology courses.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two partitioned workspaces (carrels) within a room. Partitions were painted either dark red (Munsell 5R 5/8) or light blue (Munsell 10B 7/6). A scenic picture (sunset behind mountains across a lake, 20.3 cm × 25.4 cm) was either present or absent. Task involved a simulated telemarketing reservation entry task, with either low demand (2 sessions) or high demand (5 sessions). Experiment 2 included a 90-second break between sessions 3 and 4 for the high demand task.

findings.mechanism: Low demand task leads to less attentional fatigue, thus lower negative mood.
findings.quote: when students performed the low demand task, negative mood was lower

findings.mechanism: Easier task leads to better perceived performance and higher satisfaction.
findings.quote: performance satisfaction was higher

findings.mechanism: The task was objectively designed to be low demand, which was reflected in self-reports.
findings.quote: ratings of task demand were lower

findings.mechanism: Boredom from low demand task may lead to increased feelings of isolation.
findings.quote: feelings of isolation were higher

findings.consequent: Desire to view or be viewed by others
findings.mechanism: Boredom from low demand task may increase desire for external stimulation and social interaction.
findings.quote: desire to view or be viewed by others was higher

findings.antecedent: Blue environmental color with scenic picture present (Experiment 1)
findings.consequent: Desire to view or be viewed by another
findings.mechanism: The scenic picture in a calming (blue) environment may lead to a comparative process, making individuals desire to be elsewhere or interact more.
findings.quote: when the environment was blue, individuals had a significantly greater desire to view or to be viewed by another... when there was a picture than when there was no picture

findings.antecedent: Blue environment with scenic picture present (Experiment 1)
findings.mechanism: The scenic picture in a calming (blue) environment may make the task seem more demanding by comparison.
findings.quote: slightly higher ratings of task demand... when there was a picture than when there was no picture

findings.antecedent: Red environment without scenic picture present (Experiment 1)
findings.mechanism: The stimulating red environment without a scenic picture may lead to a perception of greater privacy, possibly due to increased focus on the self or task.
findings.quote: perceptions of privacy when there was no picture than when there was a picture

findings.mechanism: Lower task demands reduce cognitive load and the likelihood of errors.
findings.quote: fewer errors occurred for the low demand task than the high demand task

findings.mechanism: Increased task duration leads to attentional fatigue and more errors.
findings.quote: fewer errors occurred in Session 1 as compared to Session 4

findings.antecedent: Low demand task, Session 4, blue environment
findings.mechanism: The calming blue environment combined with a boring low-demand task in later sessions may lead to increased boredom and lack of attention, resulting in more errors.
findings.quote: Only for the low demand tasks, though, was there a significant Time × Color interaction... only during Session 4 were more errors produced in the blue than the red environment.

findings.mechanism: Mood may be more strongly affected by task demands than by environmental design in short-term tasks.
findings.quote: There were no effects of environmental color or environmental view on positive mood

findings.mechanism: Task perception may be primarily driven by task characteristics rather than environmental features.
findings.quote: no effects of environmental color or environmental view on... task perception

findings.consequent: Perceptions of the relative amount of privacy one had available
findings.mechanism: Perceptions of privacy may be more stable or influenced by other factors not manipulated.
findings.quote: no effects of environmental color or environmental view on... perceptions of the relative amount of privacy one had available

findings.antecedent: Task type, environmental color, environmental view (Experiment 1)
findings.mechanism: Motivation may be high due to course credit and short task duration, overriding environmental effects.
findings.quote: motivation was not affected by any variables or their interaction effects.

findings.mechanism: Perceived pleasantness of the picture is stable regardless of task or color.
findings.quote: Ratings of the scenic picture also were not affected by the task or environmental color.

findings.consequent: Desire to view or be viewed by another
findings.mechanism: The scenic picture may trigger a comparative process, making individuals desire to interact more or be elsewhere.
findings.quote: Individuals had a lower desire to view or be viewed when there was no scenic picture (M = 4.5, S.D. = 2.0) than when there was a scenic picture present (M = 5.4, S.D. = 2.5).

findings.antecedent: High demand task, red environment, no scenic picture, no break (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: The stimulating red environment combined with a high demand task and no break or scenic view leads to overstimulation and increased errors.
findings.quote: individuals who performed in the red environment with no scenic picture had significantly more errors when there was no break than when there was a break

findings.mechanism: Increased task duration leads to attentional fatigue and more errors.
findings.quote: the Time effect revealed that the number of errors in Session 4 (M = 10.7, S.D. = 3.4) were significantly higher than in Session 1 (M = 5.9, S.D. = 3.8).

findings.mechanism: Cumulative attentional fatigue over the course of the task leads to increased errors in later sessions.
findings.quote: The fewest number of errors occurred in Session 3... The next largest number of errors occurred in Session 1. The most number of errors was produced in Sessions 2, 4, and 5
effect_size_assumptions: F-test has df1 > 1 (omnibus); d is an approximate directional effect.

findings.antecedent: Session 1, blue environment, no scenic picture (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: The calming blue environment may be beneficial for performance in the initial phase of a high demand task when no other visual stimulation (picture) is present.
findings.quote: errors were significantly lower during Session 1 when individuals performed the task without a picture in the blue environment rather than in the red environment.

findings.antecedent: Blue environment, scenic picture present (Experiment 2, Sessions 2, 4, 5)
findings.mechanism: The scenic picture may offset the calming effect of the blue environment, leading to more errors in later sessions of a high demand task.
findings.quote: in the blue environment, errors were greater when there was a picture present than when there was no picture present.
effect_size_assumptions: F-test has df1 > 1 (omnibus); d is an approximate directional effect.

findings.antecedent: Red environment, no scenic picture present, Session 2 (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: The stimulating red environment without a scenic picture may lead to overstimulation and increased errors, particularly in the middle of the task.
findings.quote: When performing in the red environment, errors were usually greater when there was no picture present, except during Session 2 when errors were lower with the picture present
effect_size_assumptions: F-test has df1 > 1 (omnibus); d is an approximate directional effect.

findings.consequent: Mood, performance satisfaction, perceptions of privacy
findings.mechanism: The duration of the break or task may have been too short to significantly alter these measures, or task demands may have been dominant.
findings.quote: Contrary to expectation, there were no effects of break, environmental color, or environmental view on mood, performance satisfaction, or perceptions of privacy.

findings.consequent: Self-reported looking about the environment when not entering data
findings.mechanism: Participants may not have been consciously aware of environmental effects on their looking behavior, or the task was too engaging.
findings.quote: students' reports of how much they looked about the environment when not entering data was not affected by the break, environmental color, or environmental view manipulations.

findings.mechanism: Motivation may be high due to course credit and short task duration, overriding environmental effects.
findings.quote: motivation was not affected by any of the variables.

findings.mechanism: Perceived pleasantness of the picture is stable regardless of break or color.
findings.quote: Ratings of the scenic picture were not affected by the break or environmental color.

findings.antecedent: Blue environment with scenic picture present (front carrel) (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: The presence of the scenic picture physically blocked some light in the blue carrel.
findings.quote: In the blue environment, the light readings were lower with a poster present, but only for the front carrel.

findings.antecedent: Red environment with scenic picture present (front carrel) (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: The presence of the scenic picture physically blocked some light in the red carrel.
findings.quote: The amount of lighting was fairly consistent in the red condition with and without the scenic poster.

findings.antecedent: Red environment (front carrel) with/without scenic picture (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: The red paint may have absorbed light differently or the lighting conditions were more stable in the red carrels.
findings.quote: The amount of lighting was fairly consistent in the red condition with and without the scenic poster.

mechanisms: Comparative process (individuals compare their current task situation with notions conveyed by a scenic picture, especially if the task is boring)
Restorative function (scenic views or breaks can serve a calming/restorative function, especially for high demand tasks or stimulating environments)
Stimulation/Calming from color (blue is calming, red is stimulating)
Attentional fatigue (high demand tasks can lead to fatigue, which environmental factors might mitigate or exacerbate)
Privacy perceptions (environmental color may impact privacy, which affects job satisfaction)
moderators: Environmental view (scenic picture present vs. absent)
implementation_implications: Provide scenic views in partitioned workspaces, especially for high demand tasks, or provide breaks to help control errors.
Consider environmental color: blue for calming, red for stimulating, but be aware of interactions with task demand and views.
Allow employees to personalize their workspace with pictures of family/friends or nature scenes, as these are highly desired.

limitations: The task duration (15-16.5 minutes) may have been too short to observe significant effects on mood, performance satisfaction, or motivation.
The use of students for course credit may have influenced motivation levels, making it difficult to detect environmental effects.
The high demand task might not have been demanding enough to consistently induce attentional fatigue.
Lighting levels varied between blue carrels with and without the scenic picture, which could confound results, although red carrels were consistent.
The specific scenic picture used may not be representative of all nature views, and different scenes could yield different results.
The study was conducted in a simulated environment, which may not fully generalize to real-world telemarketing jobs.

paper_metadata.title: How Movement Modulates Hearing.
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Hearing is often viewed as a passive process: Sound enters the ear, triggers a cascade of activity through the auditory system, and culminates in an auditory percept. In contrast to a passive process, motor-related signals strongly modulate the auditory system from the eardrum to the cortex. The motor modulation of auditory activity is most well documented during speech and other vocalizations but also can be detected during a wide variety of other sound-generating behaviors. An influential idea is that these motor-related signals suppress neural responses to predictable movement-generated sounds, thereby enhancing sensitivity to environmental sounds during movement while helping to detect errors in learned acoustic behaviors, including speech and musicianship. Findings in humans, monkeys, songbirds, and mice provide new insights into the circuits that convey motor-related signals to the auditory system, while lending support to the idea that these signals function predictively to facilitate hearing and vocal learning.

environmental_features: simulated urban view (e.g., city street, buildings)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: duration of the simulated telemarketing task (e.g., 30-60 minutes)
control_conditions: neutral color scheme (e.g., grey or white)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments restores directed attention and reduces mental fatigue better than urban or barren environments.
Exposure to natural environments elicits positive affective responses and reduces physiological stress.
Specific colors (e.g., blue, green, red) evoke distinct psychological and physiological responses, influencing mood and performance.

instruments_used.name: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire consisting of two 10-item mood scales, one for positive affect and one for negative affect.

instruments_used.name: NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)
instruments_used.description: A multidimensional rating scale that assesses perceived workload in six areas: Mental Demand, Physical Demand, Temporal Demand, Performance, Effort, and Frustration.

instruments_used.name: Simulated Telemarketing Task Performance Metrics
instruments_used.description: Measures such as call duration, number of successful calls, errors made, or sales conversion rates during the simulated task.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.description: Measures the variation in the time interval between heartbeats, used as an indicator of autonomic nervous system activity.

mechanism_chain.description: Natural views provide 'soft fascination' and reduce cognitive load, leading to restoration of directed attention and improved mood, which in turn enhances performance on demanding tasks. Specific colors may directly influence arousal and affective states.
